entries.text: For Tenet's inverted bullets, King didn't just reverse a gunshot recording. He split the shot into its mechanical parts (action, firing, the bullet leaving the barrel, the impact) and played those ordinary sounds back in reverse order, so you can always tell where the bullet is.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: King's team recorded Tenet's gunfire with John Fasal and Eric Potter in a canyon walled on three sides. They set mics 100 to 200 yards from the guns to pick up the long, varied echoes and reverb tails that a real outdoor space gives you.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: For Tenet's F50 hydrofoil racers, King's recordist taped 12 to 15 mics around a boat's deck in deck-coloured tape and recorded all day. The signature was a high cavitation whistle from the foils, resonating up the mast. Splashes and hull hits came from other boats, because the whistle masked everything.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: Tenet's runaway 747 runs at full jet power for a long time, so King used shifts in perspective to break up the intensity: tyre skids as the plane turns, moments where the engines drop away or change colour, and a deeper, louder sound when the camera is underneath.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: For Tenet's highway chase, the cars, including a turbocharged BMW M5, were chosen partly for their sound. To sell the low camera angle, Eric Potter recorded small road details: bumps, lane changes, running onto the shoulder, a tyre hitting a manhole cover. Drifts and skids were recorded separately for processing.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: For Tenet's inverted world, King kept literal reversal to a minimum. Wind was designed to feel like suction instead of gusts, and the seagulls were built to sound like an echo of real gulls. They found early on that simply playing elements backwards didn't feel strange or special enough.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: Much of Tenet was worldized. Fight blows, kicks and inverted explosions were played through a loudspeaker and re-recorded in corridors and rooms with interesting echo. King values the acoustic accidents this gives, which are hard to get from plugins.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: When King builds a first-pass effects track for a Nolan film, he works with the music turned off. He wants the sound field to stand on its own as a complete three-dimensional world. Effects and score are then traded off on the mix stage.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: The fast F50 boat dialogue in Tenet couldn't all be replaced. Rizzo cut ADR together with the production lines, using EQ and processing to make the ADR sound like the actors' radio mics so the two would match. The goal was clearer speech without leaving the scene's context.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: In Tenet's red room/blue room conversation, each side of the glass has a direct voice plus an intercom feed, so four voice sources in total. Rizzo and editor Jennifer Lame checked every piece so the scene would still work if fans played it backwards.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: Zenimation cuts between Disney films made decades apart. Mills used ambiences as glue through each episode. In the rain episode, he made long transitions and added extra rain, sometimes as a surround effect, to carry viewers between films from very different eras.

source.title: The Sound of Zenimation on Disney+

entries.text: Mixing Zenimation, Fluhr kept the older films narrow and centred, as they were originally mixed. He moved carefully between eras so the image never suddenly jumped to a wide format. He used several reverbs with long tails to hold onto sounds across transitions.

source.title: The Sound of Zenimation on Disney+

entries.text: Fluhr knew many Zenimation viewers listened on earbuds in bed, so he checked both the 5.1 and stereo mixes on headphones, which he never does for theatrical work. The streamer's dialogue-based loudness spec was a challenge because the show has no dialogue.

source.title: The Sound of Zenimation on Disney+

entries.text: For the research-ship crash in Alien: Earth, every member of the team tried complex layered passes on the thrusters that keep firing once the ship is lodged in a building. What worked in the end was a few chopped-up rocket recordings. Gilmore's point: pick one cool sound, not ten.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: In the crash aftermath of Alien: Earth, Gilmore started cuts with a single panicked woman before bringing up the crowd beds. One person freaking out is what motivates everyone else. Spotted call-outs layered on top gave the scene its texture.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Inside the crashed ship in Alien: Earth, the backgrounds were steam, sparks and groans, which couldn't all play at once. Gilmore scored them like music: each groan placed for a reason, steam blasts that half-sound like Xenomorphs, and muted sparks before a big one so it really scares.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Noah Hawley wanted the tick in Alien: Earth to seem to laugh at its prey. Gilmore built its chittering laugh from dolphin sounds, and Nolan McNaughton recorded his own sucking sounds for the feeding.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: On Alien: Earth, no Xenomorph close-up got a single stock scream. Every appearance was rebuilt from base layers, with performances that ramp from something like a simmering tea kettle into a hero scream, so the creature reads as angry, plotting or toying with its prey.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: For Alien: Earth backgrounds, Gilmore used dense cricket recordings he'd made in Mississippi, manipulated until they no longer sounded like crickets. He had refused to reuse Romulus sounds on the series, as he'd refused to reuse 1979 sounds on Romulus.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Alien: Earth lab backgrounds were laid as room tone first, then dressed with spotted call-and-response machines. In the transfer room, where Marcy feels safe, the backgrounds are slightly discordant to suggest something isn't right.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Approaching the crashed building in Alien: Earth, some sounds warn you what's coming. At other points Gilmore's team pulled everything out so you don't know what's next, which is why the Rottweiler barking when the tarp is pulled back lands so hard.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: For the new Prodigy tech in Alien: Earth, Davey found that the 1979-style Weyland-Yutani palette didn't fit on screen. Soft, harmonic beeps in the vein of Passengers were wrong too. The new tech had to be more seductive, but not frictionless, with an undertone of something nefarious.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: On Alien: Earth, Davey managed sound against Jeff Russo's score through frequency and texture: keep out of the bands the score occupies, and lean on density. He compares it to Smashing Pumpkins guitars, which you can turn down and they still sound massive.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Davey used Neverland's jungle backgrounds in Alien: Earth to map the island. Prettier birds play with the hybrid kids, harsher insects in Boy Kavalier's spaces, and mysterious creature growls deeper inland. Some of it came from bird, wind and tree recordings he made on his honeymoon.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: On Alien: Earth, McNaughton built the internal mechanics of Morrow's transforming arm from old recordings of a small plastic toy truck being rolled, flexed and moved. He liked its thick timbre.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: While camping in Sequoia National Forest, McNaughton recorded barbecue grills and the doors of bear-proof food lockers, with a mic placed right inside the locker. That material became source for the groans and moans of Alien: Earth's destroyed ship.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: For Alien: Earth's endless spark showers, McNaughton designed a palette of diverse, tumbling sounds with pitch movement: libraries of constants, swelly bits, one-off actions and big blasts. He weaved them together so the sparks never become one constant sound.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: For the crash crowds in Alien: Earth, McNaughton avoided wall-to-wall screaming. He cut single shouts or words fading in and out of camera perspective, using panning and reverb to place the listener in the space.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: The echolocation-like rumble of the 'orchid' creature in Alien: Earth is McNaughton's own stomach growl, pitched down with its bass harmonics emphasised.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Montaño says the Fast films live in the midrange. Impacts, guns, metal and glass can wear the audience out, so on F9 he managed them by pitching down, compressing, limiting and EQing, getting in and out of hits quickly, and leaving short breaks between them.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: In F9's action sequences, Montaño's mix goal is 'get me to Mia': clear the way for whoever is giving instructions and running the battlefield, so the audience knows where the good and bad guys are, then return to the mayhem.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: F9's electromagnets are tonal by nature, and steady tones get lost under other sounds. Montaño needed fluctuation in them to cut through, gave each vehicle's magnet its own flavour, and used addition by subtraction: hit the magnet, get out, let other things play, come back.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: For F9's Atmos mix, Montaño says full-range surrounds matter so moving objects keep their low end instead of losing it to bass management. He moved vehicles before and after they appear on screen.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: Pre-dubbing F9's dialogue, Taylor watches for sharpness. Shouted lines move from the chest into the throat, and the resulting harsh frequencies have to come out. The dialogue still has to be big enough to get through the cars and the score.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: On F9, Taylor and Frank Montaño share the console. While Montaño runs a long effects pass on the speakers, Taylor tweaks his own stems on headphones at the same time, then checks them on the big speakers afterwards.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: Files has trouble cutting without mixing. As he drops in a sound, he adds some panning and a bit of reverb right away, because that's how he judges whether the sound will actually work.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: Files mixes Stranger Things in a mid-size Atmos room. It's big enough for theatrical Atmos and for a group of clients, and detailed enough to catch problems you'd otherwise only hear on nearfields at home.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: To get through Stranger Things episodes of 75 to 150 minutes, Craig Henighan pre-mixes as he cuts. Files and Mark Paterson then pre-dub in two separate rooms for two or three days, come together to mix for a couple of days, and play it for the producer.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: Even when he has supervised and designed a film, Slater mostly takes the dialogue and music chair at the final mix instead of effects. He knows the effects already, and switching sides keeps him from being too attached to his own tracks.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: Last Night in Soho needed Soho's transformation from a daytime work district to drunken 2am chaos. Slater sent three recordists out with gear for a whole night to capture what they found, sounds you wouldn't think to ask for.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: Craig Henighan says Will Files worked out a way to send the Stranger Things mix live to an iPad, and Netflix gave the team private links. They could check how a mix translated to phones, tablets and home soundbars, then go back and adjust it.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: For Greyhound, production mixer David Wyman put a mic on every actor who speaks, about 25 isolated tracks, plus the ship's phones and loudspeakers. That way repeated orders and reactions could overlap naturally. In post, Minkler's team mostly cut from the main five or six tracks.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: Years before Greyhound, Minkler spent an hour lying in the nets on the bowsprit of a 440-foot clipper ship under pure sail at 22 knots, holding mics out over the bow wash. It was a rare chance to record a ship with no engine. That material, enhanced, went into Greyhound.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: Greyhound's backgrounds are only wind, water and turbines, so Minkler kept them changing with the story. Engine pitch rises and falls with speed orders, and the wind howls or drops as the captain walks in and out of the bridge.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: Minkler sets his limiter threshold four or five dB below peak, where many mixers use about a quarter dB. On Greyhound he aimed for big and exciting without loud, so the audience never gets pushed out of the film.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: Score plays through about 85 percent of Greyhound and uses a lot of low end. Minkler uses the sub sparingly, and to keep engines and guns distinct he keeps every element moving in level, frequency and position, so subtly that you don't notice.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: For the facehugger corridor in Alien: Romulus, the team had built complex creature vocals placed in Atmos at different reverb depths. When they muted all of it and kept only body movement and a few details, everyone agreed the scene was much better.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: After the chestburster's scream in Alien: Romulus, Files cut all music and sound. On the next shot, of the ship heading for the station, he held the silence instead of bringing sound back in. The audience freezes because the convention has been broken.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: Alien: Romulus is mixed with layers of film saturation and distortion under everything, and the opening near-silence carries film hiss, not digital zero. Silence in space is suggested by rolling off the high frequencies, which audiences accept as silence.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: To make Alien: Romulus dialogue sound like 1979, Paterson applied the film saturation to the voices too. He let loud lines physically distort, didn't tame every sibilant, gave each space its own reverb, and leaned on distant perspectives, limiting himself to what 1979 tools could do.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: In Alien: Romulus, the Corbelan launch plays with no music at all. Score comes in only once the ship stabilises, and the contrast makes it land. Paterson says that boldness of choices is what the original films' mixes were built on.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: Ripley shoots wide and holds shots long. Wherever he could, Zipf accentuated foreground sounds in the wide shots, adding to the sense that we are observing or judging Tom and creating life outside the frame.

source.title: The Sound and Music of RIPLEY

entries.text: On Ripley, Zipf synced Foley tightly to the production sound so you can't hear where one ends and the other begins. On long fixed shots he used perspective and room acoustics to mark each cut sonically.

source.title: The Sound and Music of RIPLEY

entries.text: For the Stuka dive siren in Dunkirk, King put a real air-raid siren inside a steel drum and fired it up in the desert. That was the 'pure' element. He then pushed it to be less literal, so it grows from a distant howl into a piercing, almost animal scream.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - Dunkirk - Airplanes

entries.text: For Ava Paige's vehicle in Maze Runner: The Scorch Trials, Lee slowed a distant jet recording right down for a haunting approach, then added a degausser and a Reaktor-built sound with a tearing, air-distorted quality; Atmos's full-range surrounds and bass management gave it looming size and rumble.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Maze Runner: Scorch Trials

entries.text: To make The Curious Case of Benjamin Button feel sparse and period, Klyce's team had recordist Aaron Zeller gather ambiences in New Orleans swamps and rural spots far from city noise, then built the backgrounds from those clean, unmodern recordings.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Curious Case of Benjamin Button

entries.text: Instead of a loop group for the elderly Southern voices in Benjamin Button's old folks' home, Klyce sent recordist Aaron Zeller into real care homes with tiny mics hidden in his sunglasses, pretending to read a magazine while he captured the real background chatter.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Curious Case of Benjamin Button

entries.text: Recording jungle and baboons for The Hunger Games: Catching Fire while hiking in light, Peirson ran two stereo pairs pointed away from each other about 70 feet apart, using different microphone models so the same location yields two distinct-sounding, quad-style layers.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games

entries.text: During Catching Fire, Peirson worked down the hall from the director and played works-in-progress several times a day with all music and dialogue muted, so the director heard only the effects and backgrounds being added.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games

entries.text: In Catching Fire's jungle, Peirson avoided hard ambience cuts: backgrounds sweep in up to six seconds before the next scene, and a constant canopy of leaf movement overhead runs throughout, unnoticed but adding an oppressive, claustrophobic presence.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games

entries.text: On Dunkirk, production mixer Weingarten recorded every principal boat that had a working motor as sound effects, plus boots on sand and street and harbour rigging, and even handed a small Zoom recorder to the Spitfire pilots to ride inside the planes.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - Dunkirk - Location Recording

entries.text: For the schizophrenic episodes in The Soloist, Scarabosio's team recorded a cello making notes, squeals and squawks, then processed them to sound deconstructed, mirroring the character's mind sliding from normal to unravelling; city sounds were also shaped into rhythmic patterns.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Soloist

entries.text: In The Soloist's tunnel scene, as Nathaniel starts playing the cello, Scarabosio's team let the roar of passing traffic recede and turn into gentle waves, so the world sonically falls away around him.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Soloist

entries.text: With a tiny team on All Is Lost, Proctor and Steve Boeddeker split the work by world rather than by reel: Proctor took everything Redford's character did (movement, breathing, handling the boat), avoiding overlap between editors.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of All is Lost

entries.text: Baby Driver's opening chains sounds in one key: the Sony logo ping is repitched and given an infinite reverb tail that becomes tinnitus, which hands to Steven Price's strings, and the Subaru's brake squeal, in reverse echo, sits in that key too.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - Baby Driver - Opening Scene

entries.text: For Baby Driver's Tequila shootout, where gunshot muzzle flashes had to land on the music, production mixer Ellis fed timecode to the cameras, video assist, editorial and the lighting dimmer board, even as playback speeds changed on the fly.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - Baby Driver - Tequila Scene

entries.text: For the street battles in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2, Peirson's team recorded guns among urban buildings to capture slaps and echoes, and inside a warehouse at different spots for tighter versus more open interior perspectives.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2

entries.text: The toxic oil trap in Mockingjay – Part 2 first sounded like waves and water, which felt soothing. Peirson added pitched fire elements and mud to give it weight, menace and danger.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2

entries.text: In the quiet woods scenes before the music enters in the Hunger Games films, Peirson builds the space point by point: a tree creak placed here, a single bird there, another bird elsewhere.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2

entries.text: On Tetro, Horner treated the opening minutes as a sound design overture: introducing the effects that will recur, like the light bulb inside the character's head, so the audience learns that those sounds mean they are in his mind.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Tetro

entries.text: As Benny walks through Buenos Aires's La Boca in Tetro, Horner placed a distant, ambiguous shout in the space (a fight or a street football game), giving the neighbourhood a faint edge of danger without spelling it out.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Tetro

entries.text: Horner found Tetro's Buenos Aires scooter recordings cut through the mix like a knife, so he used them wherever he could to build tension around a dialogue moment, then release it.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Tetro

entries.text: For Transcendence's Atmos mix, Porter asked the music editor for eight 7.1 stems (orchestra, percussion, harp/piano, high synth, low synth) and placed each in a different plane of the room, separating music from dialogue and effects.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Transcendence

entries.text: When Johnny Depp's uploaded character speaks from within the walls in Transcendence, Porter used Atmos to spread the voice so it commands the whole room, a booming, godlike presence he found limited in 7.0.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Transcendence

entries.text: Empire of Light's cinema was a pop-up set in a seafront tent. Wilson had it built on its own steels, not touching the tent frame, and had the glass doors fitted with thick acoustic office glass in rubber gaskets so wind vibration couldn't travel through.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: Protecting Empire of Light's quiet dialogue on location, Wilson lobbied catering to deal with food waste so seagulls wouldn't roost on the set roof, and had loud period cars choreographed to pass away from important lines.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: Because the camera never leaves the cinema during Empire of Light's riot, Wilson miked both inside and outside the glass, giving post control over how intelligible the skinheads shouting through it would be.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: For the riot in Empire of Light, Burdon muffled the skinheads' voices through the glass with EQ and a touch of glass-like reverb, keeping them very muted even when they're right at the glass, which made the moment more disturbing.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: In Empire of Light's lobby scene, with no music, Burdon kept clean production dialogue and stepped the crowd back, weaving a handful of elements down to a hush at the key line, then expanding again as the drama moves on.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: For the police breaking Hillary's door in Empire of Light, Miller built each impact from five or six elements (wood bangs, low hits, chain, door cracks), starting loud, then thinning and rebuilding so later bangs feel bigger, adding sub generators and surrounds toward the final burst.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: At the start of Empire of Light's riot, Miller disguised the passing scooters with delays, reverbs and filters so the characters (and audience) can't place them, narrow in the corridor and opening up as they step into the lobby.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: During Empire of Light's riot, Miller rolled off the top of the mob outside while creeping up the low end; when the glass breaks there's a one-frame dip, then the filters snap out and full top end returns for the crack.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: After the glass breaks in Empire of Light's riot, Miller tried playing it fully real, then filtered all effects down to nothing so the music carries the brutality; sirens return filtered and reverbed to pull the audience back to reality.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: For Empire of Light's premiere crowds, Miller used surround recordings Stuart Wilson made on set, processed through the Ambeo plug-in and panned around the room, making maximum use of material from the shoot.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: On Empire of Light, Miller used lush, soft reverb on the Foley rather than the dialogue to sell the cinema's warm spaces, keeping dialogue intelligible without heavy verb.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: Mixing Empire of Light, the team ran the whole film in about four days, made a DCP and watched it in a cinema every week, tackling story-arc sound decisions early rather than three or four weeks into the final.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: For the cinematic finisher kills in God of War Ragnarök, Jimenez borrowed film mix logic: hard effects anchored in the center, with non-diegetic whooshes and viciousness coming from the rears and travelling rear-to-front, so a short linear gameplay moment plays like a movie.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Garm, the largest creature in God of War Ragnarök, was built for 3D audio: footstep sounds are tagged to each of the four paws and other sounds fire from points along his physics-driven chain, so walking underneath him puts sound all around the player.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For giant roars like the bear Björn in God of War Ragnarök, Jimenez layered quad, more tonal echo tails on top of the positioned roar, selling the fiction that the sound propagated so hard it bounced back from distant canyons. Big impacts likewise trigger the environment: trees shaking, foliage and snow rattling.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Ingrid, the talking sword in God of War Ragnarök, was kept organic rather than digital: glass particles scattered on a bowed cymbal, recorded with a Sanken and slowed down for magic tinkle, plus ocarina and human whistles morphed together in Logic's Alchemy to form her 'voice'.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For Atreus's Sonic Arrow in God of War Ragnarök, Higa slingshotted bullet casings and paper clips in the desert, since objects that disturb the air whistle best. A whip crack recorded on the same trip became the hit-confirm transient, and ocarina tones gave the arrow a pitch players can pick out in battle.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: The energy core of the Sonic Arrow in God of War Ragnarök came from a warbly laser-bass synth patch: Higa simply EQ'd out all the synthetic high mids, leaving a smooth, chaotic motion layer he could build the arrow around.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For the elegant Light Elf assassins in God of War Ragnarök, Higa's team struck tuning forks and waved them past the mic, borrowing the lightsaber idea of a moving mic for natural Doppler, then pitched the takes way down in the sampler for slow, regal passbys.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Bifrost powers in God of War Ragnarök are used by many enemies and cinematics, so the team recorded hydrophones in tubs and canteens, stretched the sloshing, added small glassy debris, then wrote a style guide with shared source and references so every designer pulled from the same library.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: In God of War Ragnarök, ambience is sidechained to the music's RMS with very slow attack and release: as the score swells, the ambience drops in level and gets a high shelf cut, keeping its body but removing detail that would fight the notes. Combat states duck it further.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Every cinematic in God of War Ragnarök has its own custom ambience mix state, because much of what plays under cutscenes is the live in-game ambience. With the game's single unbroken camera, a hard ambience change at a transition would break immersion.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: To stop eight-enemy fights turning to mush in God of War Ragnarök, a per-frame system sorts enemies by threat: at most two sit in the high-priority bucket, while the rest are turned down and allowed to duck harder. You hear whoever is attacking you right now.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: God of War Ragnarök scales its multiband sidechaining to overall game loudness: in a quiet cavern the ambience never pumps, but the louder the game gets, the harder the real-time side chains work to clear space for story dialogue.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For the Spark of the World in God of War Ragnarök, Previty split the area into an icy, glassy tonal palette on one side and rocky lava-fire on the other. The central light's base tone is a library recording of a kids' choir warming up, cleaned, slowed down and made more tonal.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For inverted gunfire in Tenet, King pulled a gunshot's mechanics apart and reordered the forward-recorded pieces, so the bullet's story reads in reverse, ending with a punch-in-the-hand as it seats back into the casing, while the gun's own mechanism still sounds like it's running forward.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: For Tenet's final battle, King's team shot guns in a box canyon enclosed on three sides, placing mics 100 and 200 yards away to capture long reverberations and echoes that could stand in for the city environment on screen.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: On Christopher Nolan films like Tenet, King predubs the effects without playing any music, treating the effects as if they were the whole movie, so the sound world arrives at the first temp as a three-dimensional space that stands up on its own.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: Tenet's full-throttle 747 sequence needed perspective changes so the audience wasn't stuck in jet roar: tire skid detail as it turns, group after the crash, and a deeper, boomier, scarier sound when the camera is under the plane.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: For the conductor's baton tap opening Tenet, King sent Nolan 20 alternative baton taps. He rejected them all in favour of the noisy production sync tap, which Gary Rizzo then cleaned up.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: Since Dunkirk, Nolan's home releases including Tenet carry the theatrical master. Rizzo says the only change is a level compensation for home surrounds, with no separate near-field remix.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: In The Bear's kitchen, Giammaria builds backgrounds by asking what would really be happening at that time of day, say three hours before service with five people next door, then whether it serves the scene's emotion. Notes get as granular as 'fewer forks, more dishes.'

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: Giammaria treats boom and lavs on The Bear like a wet/dry blend: the boom stays in almost all the time, reinforced by lavs (auto-aligned by the dialogue editor) for the chaotic multi-actor kitchen scenes.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: For The Bear's fork-throw, table-flip and car-crash sequence, Giammaria cut the low-end thumps that ate loudness rather than drop the whole episode 2dB to fit them. Most viewers watch on TVs without full-range speakers, so the midrange has to do the work.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: Giammaria tries to keep The Bear's dynamics in check so viewers go from whispers to a car crash in 90 seconds without reaching for the remote. After the table hit he slowly backs down the screaming, watching average loudness.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: On The Bear, actors often change a take mid shouting-match, so their voices bleed into other actors' mics and alts won't match. Benjamin found RX could surprisingly peel one word off another, especially where one line ends on an S as another begins.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: For the car crash ending The Bear's family dinner episode, Scott D. Smith had a mic inside the car and one outside. Benjamin cut Mikey's screaming from the interior mic only, so the perspective came straight from production.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: With The Bear's heavily improvised shouting matches, Smith asks the actors before rolling where they'll take the scene. If he suspects it will get loud, he dials everything down and trusts post to recover quieter lines, rather than risk clipping.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: For The Bear's dozen-person family dinner, Smith miked everyone, used plant mics, ran up to three boom operators plus two utilities, and sometimes hid mics in actors' hair, working closely with hair and wardrobe.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: For long, quiet scenes on The Bear, Smith goes out of his way to get at least one take that can be boomed. Relying on lavs alone strips the perspective and life from the scene, and muffled lavs are a reason people turn on subtitles.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: The Social Network jump-cuts between two depositions, so Klyce gave each room its own dialogue reverb and room tone, one 'woody', one 'glassy'. These 'vertical edges' let the audience know instantly where they are, however frenetic the editing.

source.title: The Sound and Music of "The Social Network" Panel

entries.text: For the Ruby Skye nightclub in The Social Network, Klyce's team got the club's 2003 playlist, then made several treatments of the chosen song: a bassy one, a distorted one and a piercing 2kHz one. Stacked together in the scene, the music worked like a sound effect.

source.title: The Sound and Music of "The Social Network" Panel

entries.text: Mixing the score on The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, Klyce found a distorted growl in Reznor and Ross's stems doing the job of Salander's motorcycle. The options: tune the motorcycle to it, make both work, or drop the effect entirely.

source.title: The Music in Sound with Ren Klyce

entries.text: On the animated feature Luck, Rizzo made frequency decisions shot by shot: while the sparkly good-luck crystals occupy the extreme high end, he avoids leaning into flutes and cymbals in the score, and he'll pull back just the drums so rumbles and explosions can fill the low end.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Design behind animated feature film “Luck”

entries.text: For the NYPD helicopter's tailspin in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier finale, Patrick took steady helicopter recordings and rode the fader up and down fast for a classic chop, while pitch-shifting up and down as it spirals toward the bridge.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: Recording at home on The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Patrick used her Dyson vacuum, processed in various ways, as a core of Redwing's jet sound, both for full-speed flight and its stealth mode. Kitchen gadgets and tools became the extra articulation for Sam's new Wakandan suit.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: Redwing's chirps in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier came from small ceramic water-filled bird whistles, played as if 'talking', then run through Soundtoys Crystallizer presets, giving beeps that still hint at a bird. Nia Hansen had suggested Crystallizer for widening sources.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For Captain America's shield in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Patrick started from the classic Marvel hit, reversed and lengthened the ring-outs for throws, and added pots, pans and baking sheets to feel heavier. John Walker's fake shield used only the pots and pans, minus the Marvel layers.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: Mixing The Falcon and the Winter Soldier's action, Wild goes shot by shot asking what story each shot needs, carving fast moments into the timeline. She insists you do the work yourself rather than hear a limiter doing the mix for you.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For One Battle After Another's early chase in beat-up stock vehicles, Scarabosio made the dynamics spatial as well as level-based: cutting inside a car brings its rattles into the surrounds, and cutting outside returns the sound to the screen, following the picture cut by cut.

source.title: The Sound of One Battle After Another

entries.text: For the car interiors on One Battle After Another, García generally used a dynamic mic at low gain, which captures the transients of rattling, maxed-out vehicles well.

source.title: The Sound of One Battle After Another

entries.text: On Arcane, Eliot Connors spent much of the show crunching transients through distortion and checking them on iPhones to see what would pop. In the mage scene he left a couple of frames of silence just before the staff strikes the ground, so the magic hits you in the chest.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: Eliot Connors cut Arcane's fight scenes with single, isolated sounds rather than stacks: the spear landing, the grenade clicking in from the side, Jinx's chomper on the board. Layering, he found, creates mud and eats the frequencies the score needs, so one well-chosen sound per beat keeps both readable.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: For the Firelights' hoverboards in Arcane, Eliot Connors built a signature sound from flute recordings by a staff flautist, adding slapback delay so the flute echoes out of the tunnel. Each cut then got its own flavour: a high-pitched dirt bike, horses, mechanical clatter for the kickflips.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: For Rio, the lizard-like creature in Arcane, Eliot Connors first did a sync pass with his own voice, then blended creature calls with seal vocals. Pitching the seal down gave it a small cry that makes the audience pity it, and he let its scaly movement carry moments more than the vocals.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: To keep Arcane's Zaun from repeating itself, Eliot Connors varied the steampunk palette per scene. For a distant wide view he took a signature machine gear beat, pitched it way down and added a canyon-style slapback, and he slipped odd one-offs (a crow, pitched crickets) into gaps in the dialogue.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: Facing dense Arcane scenes, Eliot Connors cut one layer at a time: the boards one day, then mute them and do guns and ricochets, then bring everything back to cull. He pre-dubbed and panned before the stage so mixers could spend their time on dialogue, music and effects balance.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: Arcane was designed and mixed with stereo and headphones as the main target, since much of its audience are gamers. Eliot Connors checked his design on multiple pairs of headphones and cheap speakers, and at very low volume, to make sure backgrounds and one-offs still brought the world alive.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: For Arcane's hextech magic, Brad Beaumont's team built clean, pure tonal palettes that avoid sounding synthetic: soft synths layered into custom instruments, married to Eliot Connors' wine-glass recordings to keep them grounded. They agreed tuning with the composer early, so the palette could be moved anywhere and still sit with the cues.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: The Fighter's punches came from about six realistic elements varied through each fight: purpose-recorded boxing gloves on bodies, hits on meat with and without bone, and celery stalks against leather pillows. Odin Benitez's team cut different blends for body and face hits, then Myron Nettinga mixed passes for David O. Russell to choose from.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: David O. Russell rejected anything that sounded like a Hollywood whoosh on The Fighter, so Odin Benitez drew stylised moments from the real environment instead: ringing mic feedback he caught echoing round an arena, slightly processed boxing bells, and blood rushing plus Mickey's breath for the subjective corner moment.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: Every crowd in The Fighter was replaced. Odin Benitez recorded a whole fight night at the Home Depot Center over four to six hours, as tiny undercard audiences grew into the main-event crowd, with two roaming recordists. A borrowed recorder also captured the broadcast feed from ringside, corner and crowd mics.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: On The Fighter, Odin Benitez sometimes mixed a punch too loud, and David O. Russell heard that as leading the audience. One of the last fixes on the major fight sequences was pulling the punches back, though some had to stay big enough to keep the energy up.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: Library effects didn't ring true for The Fighter's Lowell neighbourhoods, so Odin Benitez's team recorded their own: a real family argument for the crack-house scene, and a helicopter he caught hovering over his own house rather than any stock helicopter.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: On a short schedule for The Fighter, Myron Nettinga pre-dubbed only the crowds, collapsing about 160 tracks into four or five 5.0 stems. Everything else stayed live on the console as automation, never printed, so ideas could still change during the final.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: When the bell rings and Dickie pulls Mickey into the corner in The Fighter's final bout, Myron Nettinga dropped the arena to a low, energetic 'dither' so the audience focuses on the brothers' speech. Even the stylised camera-flash moments avoided whooshes.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: In Woman of the Hour's cold open, Paul Stanley's team targeted winds for isolation, then let the cicadas ramp into an aggressive cacophony as the assault unfolds. Coyotes yip when they sense another predator, so that yipping is woven in more as the attack goes on and as it peters out.

source.title: The Sound of Woman of the Hour with Director Anna Kendrick

entries.text: Woman of the Hour's opening was originally full of ambience. Tony Solis pared it back to near silence to teach the audience early that silence is intentional, not a QC error. When Rodney chases Sarah, they dropped her distant screams entirely: seeing the struggle without hearing it feels more desolate.

source.title: The Sound of Woman of the Hour with Director Anna Kendrick

entries.text: For Woman of the Hour's dating-show audience, Tony Solis worked through 48-plus tracks of loop group in three layers: call-outs, a specific murmur, and cheery reactions, each with its own reverb, moving in and out. Perspective followed the character: with Cheryl we hear her view of the stage; with Rodney, his.

source.title: The Sound of Woman of the Hour with Director Anna Kendrick

entries.text: Woman of the Hour's Joshua Tree scene was fully ADR'd because of planes and wind, but Tony Solis kept the production performance and used only tiny ADR pieces to button sentences under aircraft. The effects mixers kept the centre channel clear, and ambience was just light wind, with cicadas only on the walk back.

source.title: The Sound of Woman of the Hour with Director Anna Kendrick

entries.text: To match Andor's grounded, gritty tone, David Acord gave blasters a punchier, classic-gun character and many ships a traditional jet-like sound. The diegetic approach lets the audience connect to effects in a real, visceral way rather than through Star Wars fantasy.

source.title: The Sound of Andor - Season 1 with David Acord, Margit Pfeiffer and John Gilroy

entries.text: Inside buildings on Andor, David Acord made sure a little of the exterior always bleeds in, whether a crowd or a speeder-by, so viewers stay geographically anchored on each planet. For Coruscant he reused Ben Burtt's prequel-era backgrounds, peppered with new material.

source.title: The Sound of Andor - Season 1 with David Acord, Margit Pfeiffer and John Gilroy

entries.text: Andor's Ferrix was a practical five-city-block set, and dozens of extras walking on crunchy gravel ruined the production tracks. Margit Pfeiffer's team removed that noise, replaced and looped it, and filled the trading hub with a mix of languages and accents from across the galaxy.

source.title: The Sound of Andor - Season 1 with David Acord, Margit Pfeiffer and John Gilroy

entries.text: For Fred Hampton's church rally in Judas and the Black Messiah, Skip Lievsay worked in stages. He first matched Daniel Kaluuya's mics at different distances so the voice is continuous, then built production crowds, doubling takes and adding chants. He looped a short drum beat and filtered and reverbed the music track to match production.

source.title: Judas and the Black Messiah - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: The rally in Judas and the Black Messiah is about 80% production sound. Rich Bologna's loop group mostly filled gaps, but he placed some group in the ceiling channels to make the church feel three-dimensional, and carved out some low mids so the dense tracks glued together without harshness.

source.title: Judas and the Black Messiah - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Building 1968 Chicago for Judas and the Black Messiah, Rich Bologna found almost no Black crowds in effects libraries, so loop group became essential. Diverse group performers covered the Panthers, rural white characters and a Latino gang, giving the film its authentic, naturalistic backgrounds.

source.title: Judas and the Black Messiah - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Daniel Kaluuya swung from yelling to whispering during Judas and the Black Messiah's rally speech, so Marlowe Taylor covered him with a live podium mic, a hidden plant and a boom, plus booms and XY pairs on the 350-person crowd. He also asked the director for a take where the crowd responds live.

source.title: Judas and the Black Messiah - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: For Diana and Steve's reunion in Wonder Woman 1984, shot under a semi-spherical ceiling at London's Royal College of Surgeons, Peter J. Devlin wanted acoustic foam but couldn't touch the set. Instead he floated balloons up under the dome, right above the actors, to break up its unusual acoustic.

source.title: Wonder Woman 1984 - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: In Wonder Woman 1984's playful mall opening, Gilbert Lake gave the effects a rhythm that pokes through Zimmer's jaunty score at its builds and stops. He used the walls and ceiling of the room so Diana's lasso and powers feel energetic beyond the screen.

source.title: Wonder Woman 1984 - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: For Wonder Woman 1984's mall robbery, Patty Jenkins wanted action that stayed light-hearted, so Richard King shaped the crowd reactions (Peter Devlin's recordings plus loop group) to be reactive rather than panicked. Someone pulls a gun, but it's an '80s reaction, not a modern active-shooter scream.

source.title: Wonder Woman 1984 - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Rather than ending on a battle, Wonder Woman 1984's transmission-bunker climax builds a crescendo of wind, paper, the machine and flying wishes, then turns in an instant to a subtle performance with very little sound around it. Gilbert Lake describes it as a different kind of superhero payoff.

source.title: Wonder Woman 1984 - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: The kitchen sing-along of 'Silly Games' in Small Axe: Lovers Rock is all production sync, with small pitch fixes and barely any lifts from other takes, because ADR would kill the energy. James Harrison added a little group to the later party sing-along, only to widen the colours of the vocal range.

source.title: The Sound for Steve McQueen's Small Axe - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: For Barbie's dance sequences, production mixer Nina Rice used in-ear monitors and radio mics planted in the performers' hair to capture clean sync over choreography. It took collaboration with costume and makeup; the Ken beach sequence alone needed 18 radio mics.

source.title: The Sound of Barbie

entries.text: For The Shape of Water's amphibian man, a romantic lead rather than a monster, Nathan Robitaille started from his own voice so audiences could relate. He added animal sweeteners and liquid rolls for the gills, then Guillermo del Toro recorded a breathing layer. One straight performance grew into a 64-track-wide creature.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - The Shape of Water - Creature Vocals

entries.text: When K and Joi go up to the rooftop in the rain in Blade Runner 2049, the rain starts real, then Doug Hemphill shifts it into K's head: delicate and romantic. When K gets the call from work, the real rain comes back, a change meant to be felt, not noticed.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - Blade Runner 2049 - Rain

entries.text: On True Grit, Lievsay played the voice-over narration across the left, center and right speakers while keeping on-screen dialogue in the center only. That separation gives the narration its own space, which matches where it comes from in the story.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: For True Grit's courtroom scene, Lievsay started with a realistic, warm church-like reverb on the voices. As the camera pushed in on Rooster during the prosecutor's attack, he made it louder and more reverberant, until it sounded like a preacher in a church: an effect people feel without noticing.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: Peter Kurland recorded True Grit with a boom plus radio mics on every take, and the dailies used a single mixed track. Lievsay and Byron Wilson went back to the isolated tracks line by line, since takes that sounded noisy in the mix often had one clean mic.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: No mics or cables were allowed near the horses for True Grit's river crossing, so Lievsay's team recorded horses in an equine hydrotherapy pool. The horses made almost no sound in the water except snorting to keep their noses clear. That snorting became the sound of the struggle.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: In True Grit's night cabin standoff, Mattie's footsteps on the roof were set at a level where the audience could hear them but the men inside plausibly couldn't. On the mix stage, Lievsay added one loud wooden creak, then silence, to motivate the first shot fired up through the ceiling.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: Lievsay shaped voice quality to define the characters in True Grit. For Mattie, he made her voice slightly less deep so it read clearly as a young girl next to the gruff men.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: For True Grit's back-room scene, Wilson didn't re-dub whole sequences. Jeff Bridges came back two months later and re-recorded just the words "see you" of his last line, so individual phrases could be clarified. Some lines ended up half production, half ADR.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: To capture live vocals for the concert scenes in Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere, Maitland gave the performers earpieces, kept the speakers in front of them and the audience live. He shot the close-ups first, because Springsteen's punishing register wore out Jeremy Allen White's voice after about six takes.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: For a Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere phone call with Jimmy Iovine, Maitland recorded it live with a phone-line tap, putting the on-camera actor and the incoming caller on separate tracks. He asked the actors not to overlap, because one earpiece carries both voices at once.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: To keep the Colts Neck house silent for Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere, Maitland's crew held all traffic and avoided airplanes. At the Stone Pony, by contrast, he put out as many ambient mics as he could, giving post separate room and speaker elements to blend.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: As Bruce drives faster and faster under "Frankie Teardrop" in Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere, Norris's team put Soundtoys Decapitator on the engine, moving from dry to fully wet with the acceleration. Under the song, the distortion seemed to separate from the engine and pulled the audience inside his head.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: On Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere, the team spent stage time running all the flashbacks through an Echoplex, the delay Springsteen used on Nebraska. They dropped the idea because it was distracting. The period-gear concept didn't survive the mix.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: Cleaning dialogue for Strange Negotiations, Villaflor left the steady car and room noise in. Noise is fine as long as it's smooth rather than jumping in and out and the words are intelligible, especially when the subject's voice is that distinctive.

source.title: The Sound of Strange Negotiations

entries.text: With only five days to mix Strange Negotiations, Villaflor first bulldozed a broad pass of the whole film to get something printed and confirm the emotional arc worked. Only then did he go back with the director for fine-tuning and experimental transitions.

source.title: The Sound of Strange Negotiations

entries.text: When Paul first breathes in spice in Dune, Doug Hemphill does a big frequency roll-off that pulls everything out at once. Bartlett then spun the ethereal elements around the room and added Bene Gesserit voices with spinning delays to disorient.

source.title: The Sound of DUNE with Director Denis Villeneuve and Sound Team - Featurette

entries.text: For Sound of Metal's deaf community dinner, Bladh planted mics under the tables and stuck contact mics, on wireless packs, under the surfaces with art department putty to catch the plate banging and table knocking. Post later blended these with boom and Foley.

source.title: The Sound of Metal - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Knowing Sound of Metal would mostly be watched at home, Becker's team spent real time on a separate TV/streaming mix with its own dynamics. A film that opens extremely loud makes viewers turn down, and then they miss the quiet passages.

source.title: The Sound of Metal - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: For The United States vs. Billie Holiday, Hein's team used Andra Day's own voice as a sound design element, processed until it no longer sounded like her, inside the film's emotional ambiences.

source.title: The United States vs. Billie Holiday - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: In The United States vs. Billie Holiday, the early clubs were prepped with loop group and effects so the audience talks and yells over Billie, because she wasn't famous yet. The crowds grow and quiet as her fame rises.

source.title: The United States vs. Billie Holiday - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Mixing The United States vs. Billie Holiday, Berger left the overlapping dialogue raw. He gave each cramped backstage and hotel space its own reverb combination, and used director-guided loop group lines to make every room sound specific without stepping on the performances.

source.title: The United States vs. Billie Holiday - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: After the bunker collapse in All Quiet on the Western Front, Kruse dragged contact microphones through earth for a crunchy texture, then pitched it down into an almost avalanche-like effect.

source.title: The Sound & Music of All Quiet on the Western Front

entries.text: For Oppenheimer's Trinity test, King drew on eyewitness accounts and the hum of period analog equipment to build tense anticipation. He then held silence for the roughly 40 seconds before the shockwave reached the bunker, though audiences expect to hear an explosion when they see it.

source.title: Exclusive behind the scenes featurette with the OPPENHEIMER Sound Team

entries.text: For the found-footage horror film Backrooms, Battaglia started the mix as if everything came from the camera mic, then as tension rose spilled sound design into the LCR, and only at the most intense moments opened up surrounds with camera bumps and surreal ambiences.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: Backrooms has almost no ambience: no HVAC, no air. Battaglia kept only the buzzing fluorescent lights, positioned them around the Atmos field and added reverb so you feel the size of the empty room, creating an uncanny loneliness.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: The buzzing lights in Backrooms were recorded by Umberto Corte using electromagnetic and contact mics, capturing tones and textures in the fixtures that you would not normally hear with a conventional microphone.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: On Backrooms the team found the creature scarier through incidental sounds than through screams. A peg-leg footstep became the signature danger sound, sprinkled around the space and heard progressively clearer as the film goes on.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: To keep the Backrooms creature from sounding like a generic troll or ogre, Battaglia auditioned camel vocalizations, pitched down from the start. Director Kane Parsons picked one immediately, recognizing a likeness to a Half-Life 2 zombie.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: On Backrooms some takes allowed only the camera operator and actor in the room, with 360-degree moves on 14mm and 18mm lenses. Hetmer's only option was a tiny shotgun mic mounted on the Steadicam.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: To expand R5-D4's vocal range for The Mandalorian Season 3, Collins bought a reissued ARP 2600 synth, the type Ben Burtt used, and worked classic techniques: sweeping tones, filtering and vocoding, to give the droid fear and comedic beats.

source.title: Behind the Sound of The Mandalorian (Season 3) & Obi-Wan Kenobi

entries.text: Baby Driver opens with the studio logo re-pitched so its ping rings out into an infinite reverb tail that becomes tinnitus, in the same key as the strings that follow; a car's brake squeal, reverse-echoed in that key, then leads into the first song.

source.title: Conversations with Sound Artists: 2018 Oscars Edition

entries.text: For Baby Driver's long single-take Harlem Shuffle walk, Ellis hid playback speakers behind garbage cans and plants, then killed the music for a few dialogue lines in the coffee shop, using thumpers so the actors kept the beat.

source.title: Conversations with Sound Artists: 2018 Oscars Edition

entries.text: For Baby Driver's Tequila shootout, where gun flashes had to sync with the song, Ellis fed timecode to the cameras, video assist and the lighting dimmer board, while the director sometimes changed the music's speed on the fly.

source.title: Conversations with Sound Artists: 2018 Oscars Edition

entries.text: For the amphibian man in The Shape of Water, Robitaille started from his own voice so the romantic lead felt humanoid, not alien, then added animal sweeteners, liquid-rolling gill sounds and a breathing layer from Guillermo del Toro: one channel that grew to 64 tracks.

source.title: Conversations with Sound Artists: 2018 Oscars Edition

entries.text: For the Stuka dive scream in Dunkirk, King put an air-raid siren inside a steel drum, took it out to the desert and fired it up as the pure component, then experimented to make it less literal and more like unstoppable terror.

source.title: Conversations with Sound Artists: 2018 Oscars Edition

entries.text: On tight TV and low-budget schedules, Benitez's editors pre-dub in 7.1 or Atmos rooms using clip EQ and some clip gain, so mixers get ready-made packages. Caution: clip gain hits plug-ins before processing, unlike volume automation.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: On The Night Of, Benitez worked with Steven Zaillian on choosing the exact right sound for each moment, such as the perfect door close or how a car sounds in the rain from inside, which gave a heightened feel while staying as real as can be.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: The Ultimate Playlist of Noise goes to absolute silence for a stretch, with no room tone at all. Benitez expected a QC note for a dropout, but it went through, because the silence is the story.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: Benitez urges filmmakers to have the film's own mixers do the near-field version, since that is how a film lives on, and he bought a high-end Atmos soundbar to hear how most viewers will experience the mix.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: In the horror series Them, Schultz played scenes as stark reality until a trigger moment, when everything else would peel away into heavy sound design or strange music, leading into a jump scare.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: Schultz's recorder is laid out to print every deliverable he has ever been asked for in one pass: mono comp, stereo DME, mono dialogue and effects with stereo music. Clean labelling avoids QC kickbacks.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: For Napoleon's battles, shot on about 11 cameras with up to 500 extras, Bucher recorded in three layers: one operator on a stereo-plus-centre rig for the overall battle, four costumed boom operators hidden on set, and 10 to 12 small recorders on stunt performers.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: For Napoleon and Josephine's whispered scenes, Bucher secured a VFX budget to paint out booms so they could go inside the frame. The very close, quiet dialogue then contrasts hard with the enormous battles.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: Before shooting Napoleon, Bucher tested lav positions in Joaquin Phoenix's costume and sent the files to post to agree on the best placement, then added a second mic inside Napoleon's hat, recording 32-bit float.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: On Napoleon's Austerlitz shoot, while Ridley Scott was busy filming cannon set-ups, Bucher took 100 to 200 extras 10 to 15 minutes from set to record crowd reactions, returning them when needed on camera.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: Each day on Napoleon, Bucher sorted his wild tracks and atmospheres into folders on a shared cloud system so post and picture editorial could pull them, building a location library as the shoot progressed.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: For Marie Antoinette's execution in Napoleon, Miller drew back from realistic spot effects, put reverb on footsteps, Foley and thrown vegetables to unsettle, focused on small rope details, then snapped back to reality with a huge guillotine hit.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: In Napoleon's chaotic Toulon battle, Miller kept the track full without clutter: muskets light on low end let the soldiers' stomp tracks carry weight, while off-screen cannons had top end cut and lows pushed, with mortars placed low in the Atmos surrounds.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: As the army approaches at Austerlitz in Napoleon, Miller starts with a very low-level rumble for scale, then adds top-end horse and soldier detail as they get closer. Cannon fire is precise, drawing you to individual cannonballs rather than mass chaos.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: Harrison's sound arc in Napoleon follows his strategic rise: musket and hand-to-hand sounds made for the skittish first battle at Toulon were dirty and chaotic, used only there, with later battles growing more well-oiled and structured.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: For Napoleon's coronation in a huge cathedral, Massey layered extra reverb on top of the production's natural room sound and opened it into all four corners, so Napoleon's voice fills the hall; Ridley Scott likes rich, reverberant spaces.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: Napoleon's Austerlitz runs backwards compared with a typical battle: hand-to-hand, then horse charge, then cannons, then almost no effects as the male-voice score takes over at the moment of defeat under the ice.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: To capture live singing on Wicked's Dancing Through Life, Hayes close-miked everything: two lavs, left and right, plus a boom as close as possible, so every head turn lands on a well-placed mic that sounds like a studio but keeps the effort of the performance.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: Wicked's What Is This Feeling had slamming desks, choreography and quick cuts. Hayes recorded the two leads' live vocals as cleanly as possible and wild-tracked all the background action so post could rebuild it.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: On Wicked, Nelson lays the vocals and dialogue down first as the foundation, whether talking or singing, then builds the orchestra, rhythm tracks, Foley and crowds around them.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: For Wicked's musical numbers, regular loop group actors got lost in the rhythmic sections, so Nugent Title worked with the choreographer to cast real dancers, who learned the rhythms and performed syncopated crowd vocals with the music.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: On Wicked, Marquis worked with click tracks from start to end of every reel, so effects in songs like Dancing Through Life could play with and against the music like another percussion instrument.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: To give Oz a slightly strange flavour in Wicked, Marquis used a collection of gamelan instruments, metallic, mildly tuned tones, sprinkled through scenes, along with rhythmic, tuned effects in What Is This Feeling.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: The Wizard's giant head in Wicked had to fill a cavernous chamber yet stay intelligible. Through several temp iterations Marquis balanced low end filling the space against clarity, and Andy Nelson finished dialling it in.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: Ferrari shot with modern four-cylinder replica cars, so Lamberti's team recorded the real period cars, including Nick Mason's Maserati 250F, a Lancia D50 and a 1953 car standing in for the 315, raced hard on a UK track.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Before the recordings, Lamberti, Michael Mann and stunt coordinator Robert Nagle spotted every race scene in Ferrari, including off-camera testing during dialogue: a downshift here, acceleration there. The real recordings then plugged straight in.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: In Ferrari's Mille Miglia duel, Lamberti played the camera's car, de Portago's V12, as primary and, when cars ran side by side, panned the V12 and the Maserati's throaty V8 hard left and right to clear space.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Once the real Maserati recordings arrived for Ferrari, Lamberti and Andy Nelson found they carried so much power they did not need to be played very loud to feel powerful.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Because the replica cars on Ferrari sounded wrong, Orloff chose mics to keep their engines out of the dialogue tracks so post could lay authentic engines underneath. He also had actors speak up as if over the period engines.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: For in-car dialogue on Ferrari's race scenes, follow vans were often impractical at speed, so Orloff relied on recorders embedded in the cars, using RF where in range.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Ferrari's pivotal office scene was planned with a rain pumper over a plastic-roofed built set. Orloff asked Michael Mann for a rehearsal with the rain on; it was replaced by wetting the windows and rain lighting effects.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: For Ferrari's live opera scene, Orloff recorded the singers on boom rather than lavs, which gave more of the space, in only two takes. Wide shots used pre-records, and singers heard the pre-recorded orchestra on earwigs.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: For Ferrari's rain-soaked dialogue by the car, Lee Orloff shot a wild take of the key lines without the rain machines. Weiser's team used that clean track and put rain back on top.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: To make heavily accented performances clearer in Ferrari without ADR, Weiser's team sometimes moved a single syllable a few frames within a word, keeping the actor's own performance.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: On Ferrari, Weiser premixed selected ADR takes and put them in Michael Mann's Avid alongside the original, so Mann could hear how it would sound and decide faster.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: For Ferrari's pit crews, Weiser cast an all-northern-Italian loop group, including a man from Modena, and had a period pit-crew adviser script the Italian lines and racing protocol.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: In Ferrari's church scene, intercut with a Maserati time trial, there was a close-up of one or two stopwatches. Nelson and Tony Lamberti added about 20 more, so the whole congregation seems to be timing the run.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Ferrari's opera scene begins offstage with the sound drifting through, then the full ambience of the hall; once on stage Nelson dried up the acoustic to make it intimate, which sets up the audience's reflective flashbacks.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Nelson and Tony Lamberti spent a lot of Ferrari's mix in 7.1 and 5.1, so the Atmos mix never relied on choices that would fall apart in the formats most theatres play.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: At the Mille Miglia start in Ferrari, after cheering crowds, revving engines and Enzo's pep talks, the track goes very quiet as Enzo walks away from the last driver, putting the audience inside his head.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: For the addiction montage in The Social Dilemma, Gould noticed the iPhone unlock sound resembled a shotgun cocking, so he cut it on the documentary side and followed it with a punchy, shotgun-like impact on the Pinterest logo, later dialling back the 'gunniness' in the mix.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: In The Social Dilemma's quick-cut addiction sequence, Gould built a fly-through-the-eyeball whoosh from the Mac Mail 'send' sound, layered with notification sounds and a Formula One car pass to make it more dramatic.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: For a shot of liquid rushing through veins in The Social Dilemma, Gould layered casino slot-machine dings to tie screen use to gambling, and pitched them to the music so they landed as a clean hit at the end of the phrase.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: Gould pitched the AI server room tone in The Social Dilemma to clash with the score through the film, then retuned it to the key of the music's final resolve when the code is rewritten and the room turns simpler and more natural.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: The avatar in The Social Dilemma got a busy sound when it was a vague human shape, and Gould simplified it as the visuals sharpened until it vanished. For the AI's last line he removed the vocal processing so the plain human voice landed as a contrast.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: In The Invisible Man's opening escape, the team first played the waves loud to cover Cecilia's sneaking, then reversed it: they pulled the waves out so she suddenly felt exposed. Files says nearly every mix decision followed her point of view.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: At the bottom of the hill in The Invisible Man, the music drops from huge to quiet and odd crickets play, then cut out when Cecilia turns around. Files says it leaves it open whether someone is there or her focus shifted, and it makes the audience feel she's alone.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: For the camera-covered suit in The Invisible Man, the team fed camera clicks and servos into the particle-based Sound Particles software, multiplied and randomised by the thousand, until it sounded almost insect-like. They used only tiny tastes of it when Cecilia senses something.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: On The Invisible Man, P.K. Hooker ran room sounds such as a cricket through the invisible man's suit-voice processing. When the camera settles on a spot, the faint warping hints that something stands between the sound and the lens.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Scenes in The Invisible Man with motion-control cameras and a green-suited performer had noisy production tracks, so Files's team deleted them and rebuilt each scene from scratch. That gave them animation-style control to swap levers: big music, then effects, then everything out.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Files and composer Benjamin Wallfisch put The Invisible Man score into Atmos with 'emotional panning', swinging elements through the ceiling and rear so things swim around Cecilia's head. They checked that the sense of movement through the audience still survived a 5.1 fold-down.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Files mixed The Invisible Man for contrast, like the quiet verses and loud choruses of a Pixies or Nirvana song. Sometimes the contrast came from level, sometimes from frequency, and often from stripping things away just before a big moment.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: For the restaurant killing in The Invisible Man, Hooker's team changed nothing in the mix when the throat is cut. There's no sting, the music keeps playing, and the sound only starts to change as Cecilia takes in what happened.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Joker: Folie à Deux was mixed in Atmos, but Van der Ryn's team kept the animated cartoon opening vintage, front LCR only. The narrow image made the cut to the first full-Atmos Arkham corridor feel much bigger.

source.title: The Sound of Joker: Folie à Deux

entries.text: For Arkham in Joker: Folie à Deux, Aadahl and Van der Ryn recorded guerrilla-style on Alcatraz around the tourists, capturing cell doors and smeared, blurry echoes. They used the echoes for the corridors of E Block, the solitary-confinement wing, to set it apart from Lee's block.

source.title: The Sound of Joker: Folie à Deux

entries.text: For the 'I Love Rocky Road' bar scene in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Gallagher recorded about 30 friends singing the song at a party. He ran around them with an iPhone stereo mic to get moving stereo, then layered it with loop group under Daniel Radcliffe.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: In the LSD sequence of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Gallagher pitched the tonal industrial-shredder effects to the actual notes of the score. Because nothing clashed, the mixer could push the effects hard alongside a dense score.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: At the peak of the loud LSD sequence in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Solis tried pulling a master fader all the way down as a test. Absolute silence worked better than the usual low drone or bed, and they kept it.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: Because the songs in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story were re-recorded with separate stems (even the accordion's left and right hands), Solis placed them in Atmos to suit each venue. Drums came out of the PA in the dive bar, and the outdoor number stayed dry without going flat.
