source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: For a tape-rewind gag in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Gallagher found that reversing the film's dialogue sounded bad, while reversed music worked. He layered a reversed copy of Al's Nine Inch Nails-style parody 'Germs' under the effect.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: On Nomadland, Seivers didn't treat the environmental sound in the production tracks as a problem to scrub out. He avoided heavy noise reduction and EQ, kept some signal noise for its vérité feel, and Sergio Díaz designed winds that blended with the production sound.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: On Nomadland, Seivers moved away from sending correlated sounds to the surrounds. He used decorrelated, discrete sounds that aren't shared across channels, which builds immersion without drawing attention, and made the near-field mix and downmix come together quickly.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: In Nomadland, interiors sat mostly up front while exteriors let wind, insects and cicadas spread around the room. Seivers says the surrounds were almost never a general bed; Sergio Díaz designed specific sounds for specific surround positions.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: Díaz planned Nomadland's design in three levels: the van interior kept prominent to stay close to Fern, layers of different winds for her journey, and deliberate silence, as when she wanders lost among the Badlands rocks.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: On Nomadland, Seivers and Díaz delivered the film to the director in 30-minute sections, each a near-complete temp mix. By the final mix they could sit back, watch long stretches and make broad, audience-level decisions instead of fixing details.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: For the crashed-plane scene in The Midnight Sky, Thom used the wind as cover for rhythmic metal tapping that is never seen on screen, which hints at the violence of the crash. The tapping stops dead when Augustine finds the sick man inside.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: In The Midnight Sky's plane scene, the mixers started big and wide outside, then pulled sound back as Augustine climbed in, so the audience had to lean in. Backgrounds were taken down and out to almost nothing until the gunshot brings the scene back.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: For the asteroid strike in The Midnight Sky, Thom's team rolled large boulders down hills into various objects, then muffled the impacts outside the ship. The aim was a nod to soundless space: what the astronauts feel through their bodies and hear over comms.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: On The Midnight Sky spacewalk, Foley was recorded flat in case the director rejected the treatment, then muffled and made bass-heavy in post to suggest bone conduction. Thom admits the processing was simply a low-pass filter, and they introduced the effect gently.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: When blood appears in the astronaut's helmet in The Midnight Sky, the mixers slowly faded out every ship hum and exterior sound until only her breathing inside the helmet was left, making the moment claustrophobic.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Thom says George Clooney re-voicing the younger Augustine sounded odd, and pitch shifting and voice-alikes didn't work either. In The Midnight Sky, Ethan Peck's lines are an AI deep-learning blend of Peck's and Clooney's voices.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: On Coup 53, Murch pre-mixed the composer's 22 music stems against dialogue and effects in his Premiere picture timeline while he cut. A violin never fought a key line, so the final mixer mainly had to place the music in 5.1 and set overall levels.

source.title: The Role of Art and Technology with Walter Murch

entries.text: Murch questions panning dialogue to the rear across cuts, as in Roma's bedroom scene, where off-screen voices come from behind. He finds that in a cut scene, dialogue kept centred is still heard as coming from the character, while music sources can be panned.

source.title: The Role of Art and Technology with Walter Murch

entries.text: On a William Kentridge series with very reverberant location audio, Murch tried the de-reverb tool built into Premiere and found it tunable enough to remove the ringing while keeping some natural room, an exception to his rule that fixes work only when you don't need them.

source.title: The Role of Art and Technology with Walter Murch

entries.text: On Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, Ellis and Shaughnessy Hare check Godzilla's footsteps and roars by feeling their own chests on the stage. She says that physical check translates to home viewing, and that big is easy while believable is the hard part.

source.title: The Sound of Monarch: Legacy of Monsters

entries.text: For the 'oner' battle in Deadpool & Wolverine, Henighan's team first stripped out Deadpool and Logan's on-set and ADR shouts, then hired over 50 loop group actors to give the featured kills their own sounds, before building effects in passes.

source.title: Deadpool & Wolverine - The Oner Sound Breakdown

entries.text: Henighan built the effects for Deadpool & Wolverine's oner fight in layers. First came on-screen basics (claws, swords, punches, blood, dismemberment), then gunfire such as the gold .50-cal Desert Eagles, then body and limb falls from Foley backed with effects.

source.title: Deadpool & Wolverine - The Oner Sound Breakdown

entries.text: For the TRON: Legacy light cycles, Boeddeker's fully synthesized bikes sounded too clean, so he flipped the approach: Ducati recordings given radical pitch manipulation so the Dopplers swept from very high to very low, then blended with the synthetic versions shot by shot.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: On TRON: Legacy's light cycles, Boeddeker used 'resonant sweeping', borrowed from DJ filter sweeps: a resonant filter tracks the engine's pitch as it passes, adding a high-tech whine. When a bike slowed to a stop, following the sweep down made it feed back on itself, and he kept the accident.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: For the TRON: Legacy discs, Boeddeker built a pulsing tone so the Doppler would read as it flew. To give it movement, he played the tone through his design-room speakers and waved a handheld microphone in front of them, capturing natural acoustic motion as the basis of the sound.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: For TRON: Legacy's de-rez deaths, Boeddeker had the programs scream as they died so there was something to process: he automated in a 'shuffle' plug-in that particle-izes the voice, then added a crispy effect at the end to make it sound tiny.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: In TRON: Legacy, the sound of a rider transforming into a light cycle, with tiles snapping together, came mainly from flipping through a deck of cards. Boeddeker noted that a deck of cards pushed into the subwoofer sounds really cool.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: For a recurring kettle in Demonic, McNaughton recorded his own teapot and added a hydrophone to get a thicker low texture to blend in. He also recorded its switch on several mics at different perspectives so the moment it clicks off would land.

source.title: The Sound of Demonic with Director Neill Blomkamp

entries.text: For Demonic's bird-like demon, Rossi first built a base vocal profile defining the shriek's attack and release, then layered other material into it: cracking ice for crackle, shrieking metal for high accents and slimy gurgling goo holding the bottom end together.

source.title: The Sound of Demonic with Director Neill Blomkamp

entries.text: On Demonic, Rossi sent work-in-progress mixes of his creature to Foley, dialogue and the other sound designer about every two weeks. Everyone could see what he was covering, so they built complementary layers instead of duplicating sounds.

source.title: The Sound of Demonic with Director Neill Blomkamp

entries.text: For dialogue in Demonic's first CG simulation scene, Renaud ran a delay through a flanger and spun it around the room in the Atmos/7.1 mix. Once the full mix was in you didn't consciously hear the delay, only a sense of weirdness.

source.title: The Sound of Demonic with Director Neill Blomkamp

entries.text: Boyes recorded jungles worldwide for Avatar and warned about masking: a jungle works like an orchestra, and adding one or two elements too many breaks it. Building Pandora's ambience was a careful balance of how many layers to let play.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: Avatar's viperwolves combined coyote pack-hunting yips, recorded in Malibu and in a sound editor's backyard, with hyenas recorded at a UC Berkeley research facility. Boyes shaped them into a cross between a ferocious canine and a big cat.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: Avatar was mixed in 2D, so the mixers watched each reel in 3D with James Cameron, silent and close to the screen. Cameron called out what came off the screen, and they carried that spatial memory back to the stage to make sure those sounds came through.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: In Avatar's thanator chase, James Cameron stopped the mix because he couldn't hear Jake breathing under the roars and the music. Keeping the hero's panicked breath audible kept the scene about the character rather than just a big monster sequence.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: Mixing music for Avatar, Nelson found that the 3D glasses seemed to flatten the score onto the screen. From day one he pulled the strings and shakuhachi flutes about 10 to 20 percent off the screen into the room for a more immersive feel.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: Explosions in How to Train Your Dragon were deliberately heavy in low frequencies. That let them feel powerful and shake the whole environment without being ear-piercingly loud, which they would have to be if the intensity came from mids and highs.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: How to Train Your Dragon used 'virtual pre-mixing': every candidate effect sat in sync in a Pro Tools session, uncommitted, until the final mix. Since the final score often arrives on day one of the final, the effects could still be reshaped to fit the music.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: In dense battles like How to Train Your Dragon's finale, Thom picks or builds sounds that change pitch over time, such as flybys and fire breaths. A pitch sweep grabs the ear in a way steady-state noise can't, so it cuts through without just turning everything else down.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: Building the dragon voices for How to Train Your Dragon, Thom performed with his own voice to bridge gaps. He would mimic a tiger snarl closely enough to pass as the same creature, then steer it into a sympathetic beat a tiger can't give you.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: For Toothless in How to Train Your Dragon, Thom and Al Nelson used horse breathing, including recordings of mares giving birth, for labored, emotional breaths. They pitch-shifted their own voices for the comic moments and used the subwoofer to make him sound bigger than he looks.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: If you really want to impress me send me creature vocalizations

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: For How to Train Your Dragon's dragons, Nelson mixed animal vocals with non-animal sources such as squeaking styrofoam, rubber balloons, violins and slurpy liquids. A sea lion or walrus would be the base, and bowed metal or a squeak pushed it into a squeal.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: On How to Train Your Dragon, Rizzo found that Jay Baruchel's unusually narrow frequency range needed more compression than expected to sit in the mix. Containing it let Hiccup's voiceover cut through without getting too bitey.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: Under the How to Train Your Dragon opening voiceover, Rizzo moved the score's brass out of the way while keeping the percussion. The narration stayed on top, the low-end explosions kept their weight and the pulse of the sequence never dropped.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: For the Owlship in Watchmen, Hecker layered jets and whines, then added a complex midrange synth tone run through an Eventide pitch plug-in. He mapped the pitch to a fader on a Command|8 so he could perform the rises and falls to picture.

source.title: Watchmen Sound Panel

entries.text: Dr. Manhattan's subliminal presence in Watchmen was built from whale song, chosen over throat singing and waterphone for its natural chorusing and rising and falling pitch. Hecker's team pitched, slowed and bent it per scene to track his arousal, anger and wonder.

source.title: Watchmen Sound Panel

entries.text: In Watchmen's tenement fire, Hecker's team pulled all the sounds inward, leaving a beat of silence just before the big explosion so it could land. The scene was otherwise so loud that creating ebb and flow was the main challenge.

source.title: Watchmen Sound Panel

entries.text: Watchmen has four big fight scenes, and Hecker's team kept the punches and crashes from feeling repetitive by giving them pitch and tone. Each fight got its own stylization, so even cut together they would sound distinct.

source.title: Watchmen Sound Panel

entries.text: For WandaVision's sitcom episodes, Dupre ran split stems of real period shows through a spectrum analyzer and matched their frequency response. Then she dropped the full TV-speaker sound, which pushed viewers away, in favor of an aged ambient noise bed and very sparse effects.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: WandaVision's first episodes were mixed in mono, everything stacked in the center. Only subtle hints of a world outside the sitcom spread into stereo, until the episode 3 shift to color opened the mix into the surrounds.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For the WandaVision finale's choking townspeople, Dupre layered the vocals through treatments that included compressors emulating constricting throats. Because of streaming loudness specs, she had to hold back the crowd build so Wanda's magic still had room to be the big dynamic moment.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: WandaVision's finale crowd went through three or four loop-group recording passes as the cut evolved. The first passes were too big and angry. The final version layered many subtle choking sounds and heavy breathing into a pad that didn't intrude.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For Vision and the twins glitching apart in WandaVision, Orlando layered two different Dehumanizer presets, one glitchy, over the unprocessed voices. Dialogue could break up while the performances stayed intact.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: To separate Agatha's magic from Wanda's in WandaVision, Orlando built it from the cicada sound in her lair, plus other insect buzzes and fire, avoiding Wanda's sparkly tones. Agatha's power-absorption effect started as literal water-sucking recordings, then processed.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For White Vision in WandaVision, the director asked for something based on Ultron. Whittle started from Lora Hirschberg's Ultron voice presets and made several variations, Steve Orlando added more processing, and the director picked version four.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For the station clocks in Hugo, Gearty found the real antique clocks he planned to record were all quartz-driven with no mechanisms left. Instead he recorded individual ticks from many sources and built each clock by repeating those ticks, giving every clock its own character.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: For Hugo's automaton, Gearty learned the real machine made virtually no sound, so its whole mechanical voice was invented by trial and error over weeks, then extended as the CGI internals kept changing between versions.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: On Hugo the boom was often swamped by set steam, so Stockton leaned on radio mics, de-crackled clothing noise and EQ'd out steam. When a lone line sat in a long quiet stretch, he ramped the noise up slowly into the line and back down, using visible steam bursts to justify it.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: Scorsese loved Hugo's automaton production track, which carried modern servo whine. Stockton cut it but kept it muted under Gearty's designed mechanism, unmuting pieces only when asked, so the paper-scraping survived while the servo was notched out and used sparingly.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: Hugo's automaton-room dialogue was very noisy and the filmmakers refused to loop it. Fleischman's fix: Eugene Gearty spotted small steam effects wherever steam appears on screen, so the noise in the production track reads as part of the scene.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: In Hugo's Méliès studio montage, Scorsese had Fleischman pull everything out of the track at the moment Méliès speaks to the boy, so one line of dialogue lands in sudden isolation inside an otherwise dense montage.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: Mixing Hugo in 7.1 for its 3D release, Fleischman pulled the station inspector's dialogue off the screen as his head pushes out toward the audience, matching the 3D image instead of leaving the voice locked to the center.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: On Parenthood, with 14 regulars who improvise and paraphrase, Allen records every angle the same way, always capturing off-camera dialogue, with booms plus a wireless iso for every actor on a multitrack, so lines rarely need looping.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: Production Sound Mixer Nicholas Allen

entries.text: Allen chooses wire placement after watching rehearsal for physical business, such as hugging, carrying bags or turning in a car. He won't EQ a voice unless placement colors it, and has his boom op keep wires clear of clothing so they match the boom's sound.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: Production Sound Mixer Nicholas Allen

entries.text: On 42, when the loop group and production tracks lacked a crowd reaction, like the stands responding to Pee Wee Reese embracing Jackie Robinson, Johnson's crew put up a mic on the dub stage, gathered everyone available, recorded it themselves and tripled it into the mix.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound and Music of 42

entries.text: For Nina's double in Black Swan, effects editor Wayne Lemmer mined the production dialogue for stray breaths and giggles. Henighan's team manipulated them into a reversed breath-and-giggle motif, first heard under the opening title, that returns whenever the double surfaces.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Black Swan

entries.text: In Black Swan's kiss between Cassel and Portman, Henighan built a low-end throb and an insect-like texture that rises underneath, then paid it off when Nina bites him by bringing back the established breath-giggle motif, hinting the double has emerged.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Black Swan

entries.text: With little time for recording on Black Swan, Henighan's team made Foley-style recordings of bird wing flaps, flesh sounds, tree bark, and dirt mixed with ground-up rocks, twisting and manipulating them as raw material for Nina's transformation.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Black Swan

entries.text: For Black Swan's club scene, Henighan had loop group scream 'Nina', 'mommy' and other words drawn from the film's dialogue, swirled them around the room while Nina was alone, then stutter-edited the crowd and drove it around the theatre to push into the next scene.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Black Swan

entries.text: Boeddeker's first Tron: Legacy light-cycle sounds were purely synthetic. Adding Ducati motorcycle passbys gave them grit and weight, so he switched to real bikes heavily processed: doppler bys pitched far higher in and far lower out than natural, plus filter sweeps for a synthetic feel.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of TRON LEGACY

entries.text: Mixing Tron: Legacy in 7.1, Rizzo sold big arena spaces with delays, slaps and repeats travelling across the room. For intimate scenes he kept discrete ambiences and used different reverbs on dialogue in the front, sides and rear to define the space.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of TRON LEGACY

entries.text: Tron: Legacy's light-up suits put a whine on all the production dialogue. Whittle's team cut it clean first, sent it for specialised spectral noise removal, then ran cleanup passes at the premix and again at the final, rescuing most of the production.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of TRON LEGACY

entries.text: For Smaug in The Hobbit, Boyes handled the growls, bellows, rumbles and fire breathing while Michael Hedges mixed Cumberbatch's voice. Boyes interleaved them, so the growls emerge as the voice recedes and never step on a word.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of The Hobbit

entries.text: On Toy Story 3, Semanick used the new 7.1 side walls to ease dialogue just off the screen, slightly left or right, without putting voices on the back wall, creating better spaces for characters and music.

source.title: The Sound of “Toy Story 3”

entries.text: Because Monsters University is a prequel, Myers didn't reuse Monsters, Inc. technology sounds as-is: he took those ideas and degraded them, making them rougher and more low-tech for an earlier era.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: For Monsters University's campus, Myers' team recorded ambience in the quad, cafeteria and stadium at Berkeley to capture college-campus enthusiasm, while watching that too much intelligible English didn't creep into the backgrounds.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: Pixar films pan dialogue more aggressively than live action, Myers says. Because the voice recordings are so clean, a voice can go wherever its character moves, with dialogue mixers adding perspective and reflections, as on Monsters University.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: In Monsters University's Toxicity Challenge, Myers put the loop-group crowds in the overhead and surround speakers. He removed a glow-urchin ambience because it muddied Randy Newman's dense score, keeping only specific urchin flybys and stings.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: Premixing Monsters University in Atmos with Gary Summers, Myers found that with many characters and busy music the screen piles up fast. Moving music and other elements slightly off screen cleaned up the on-screen dialogue.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: For the Bat in The Dark Knight Rises, King started with helicopters. Ken Johnson then took the head off a weed whacker and fitted different things to spin, and processed versions became a major element. The final vehicle drew on about five 'food groups' of merged sounds.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound and Music of The Dark Knight Rises

entries.text: Bane's mask hid Tom Hardy's mouth, so The Dark Knight Rises team exaggerated the clarity of his voice. Early experiments added fluid through tubes, breathing and gaseous layers, but they made him harder to understand, so King's team stripped them out and kept the voice largely natural.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound and Music of The Dark Knight Rises

entries.text: For Interstellar's truck chase through the cornfield, King's crew paid to mow down a real field with a pickup fitted with a metal bumper 'corn catcher', mics mounted behind it and inside the cab, driving repeated five-second runs.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: For Interstellar's dust storms, one of King's recordists built a sand gun, blasting gravel, sand and debris at an old junk truck; those hits combined with wind recordings sell the storm buffeting the vehicles.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: Nolan wanted Interstellar's production dialogue with almost no looping, only six to eight lines. Dialogue editors Hugo Weng and Bob Kaiser cut it like sound effects, dropping in syllables from other takes to articulate words better.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: For Interstellar's ship shakes, King's team put PA speakers and subwoofers in an aircraft-boneyard fuselage fed by two oscillators, running sine waves in and out of phase from below 15 Hz upward until the plane shook. It was the film's only synthesized sound.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: Interstellar's violent launch buffets needed character beyond a dropped aircraft wing, so Ken Johnson spent weeks recording a vibrating table loaded with metal to get layers of small rattles.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: Nolan banned hums, drones and bleeps from Interstellar's spacecraft so it wouldn't feel like Hollywood sci-fi. King's ship interiors use the room tone recorded on set: the crew's office, where they'll live for years.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: For The Social Network's backgrounds, Klyce's team sent recordists to Boston and the Stanford campus, and hid microphones inside real Silicon Valley tech offices to record authentic ambiences for the Facebook office scenes.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Social Network

entries.text: Poppe scouted Need for Speed's cars at car meets with an iPhone, judging rough samples on studio speakers. He then recorded each car in the quiet desert, 'like a drum set', with about ten mics on supercharger, intake, three or four on the muffler, sides and interior.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Need for Speed

entries.text: Recording Need for Speed's cars, Poppe relied heavily on dynamic mics, which handle the sound pressure, and on omnis because they're less wind-sensitive. Wind distortion was the one thing to avoid at all costs, since it ruins the signal.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Need for Speed

entries.text: For Terminator Salvation, Frankley banned servos and classic robot sounds. He recorded metal under stress, including metal slowly crushed in a log splitter, then processed those grinds to articulate the Terminators' movements.

source.title: The Sound of Terminator Salvation

entries.text: For Terminator Salvation's debris, Frankley ran a blower on a variac outside a stage, hosed into a tent inside, and blew sand and ground walnuts and almonds against metal, glass and canvas. Those were panned and traced through the winds.

source.title: The Sound of Terminator Salvation

entries.text: To give Terminator Salvation a family Skynet signature, Frankley ran much of the machine design through analog guitar pedals, including a ring-modulating wah, the Snarling Dogs Mold Spore.

source.title: The Sound of Terminator Salvation

entries.text: Terminator Salvation's Moto-Terminators first sounded too slick. McG asked for Harleys, so Frankley recorded a Ducati and an MV Agusta with modified exhausts on a trailer-mounted dyno in the open desert, free of reflections.

source.title: The Sound of Terminator Salvation

entries.text: For The Last of Us's clickers, blind infected who hunt by echolocation, Kovats and Derrick Espino workshopped vocals with actors until Misty Lee hit a tight, back-of-the-throat click. Kovats learned to emulate it and became the male clicker; heard unseen, echoing down a hallway, the benign click turns terrifying.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound and Music of The Last of Us

entries.text: The Last of Us used an in-house 'stochastic obstruction' system: every game frame it threw out roughly 1,500 to 2,500 random raycasts purely for audio, spending a real chunk of the PS3's Cell processor to model how walls and objects occlude sounds in its environments.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound and Music of The Last of Us

entries.text: On Brave, the first Atmos film, Rydstrom mixed traditionally in 7.1 first, then took the final-mixed material and turned individual sounds and dialogue lines into objects. Five screen channels instead of three let dialogue and effects panning across the front become far more specific.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Brave

entries.text: In Brave's brawl among the Scottish lords, Rydstrom flung thrown men and sheep overhead as Atmos objects. Elsewhere King Fergus stands on a table while the triplets hide underneath; putting Fergus's voice in the ceiling matched their point of view so naturally nobody notices.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Brave

entries.text: What first struck Rydstrom about Atmos on Brave was full-range, bass-managed surrounds: ambiences, door creaks, arrow-bys or dialogue moved behind the audience now sound as full as the screen. Even Brave's unaltered 7.1 mix played better in the Atmos room for that reason alone.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Brave

entries.text: For Real Steel's arena crowds, Henighan used the two days the production had 1,000 extras in Detroit and ran them like a loop group ADR session: a recordist with a written 'grocery list', director Shawn Levy on megaphone calling chants of robot names like Adam, Zeus and Ambush, plus cheers, all layered and manipulated later.

source.title: The Sound of Real Steel

entries.text: For the twinkling stars in The Little Prince, Nielsen rattled Goodwill glassware, light bulbs and chandeliers before recalling David Farmer's obsidian chime recordings. He hunted down thin obsidian needles sold for Native American needlework and hung them as a mobile: part metallic, part glass, very pure, then manipulated them into every star sound.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Little Prince

entries.text: The Aviator's biplane in The Little Prince combines a 1937 Waco that Nielsen recorded in Santa Rosa, used mostly for idles, with vintage biplane recordings Richard Beggs had made years earlier, which Nielsen persuaded Beggs to share; the in-flight passbys layer Beggs's material with other elements.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Little Prince

entries.text: Because the Little Prince's desert had to feel lonely and sparse, Nielsen built new winds out of paper, blurring Foley and effects; he and Foley artist Heikki Kossi spent weeks gathering every kind of paper to find what suited a world whose dunes are literally made of pages.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Little Prince

entries.text: Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol had loads of Russian dialogue shot with Czech actors. Whittle had St. Petersburg-born Skywalker colleague Mika Makarov watch the whole film flagging accents and wrong phrasing for replacement, then brought him to Tom Cruise's ADR sessions to coach his Russian.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound and Music of Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol

entries.text: For Ghost Protocol's Burj Khalifa climb, Whittle's team salvaged production breaths and efforts, which are usually the first things lost. Scenes not shot on noisy IMAX cameras, like the hotel room, were cleanly recorded enough that much production dialogue survived into the final track.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound and Music of Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol

entries.text: For Avatar's banshees, Boyes recorded two- and three-day-old piglets whose cries were unidentifiable; pitched down slightly with echo they turned birdlike, and he added guttural breathing from horses and assorted reptiles to build clucking, trilling calls and huge cries that carry across Pandora's canyons.

source.title: The Sound of Avatar

entries.text: Building creature vocals on Avatar, Boyes gathers sounds from many animals like soup ingredients, then deliberately forgets their sources. He loads them into a patch on his synth and plays with how the elements fold in and out of each other, so no single animal reads.

source.title: The Sound of Avatar

entries.text: Avatar was mixed entirely watching 2D picture, then checked in another room against the 3D image; Boyes rarely needed changes. Only specific moments were reworked, such as a bullet that comes off screen left and must whiz around behind the audience to the right.

source.title: The Sound of Avatar

entries.text: On Avatar, Boyes didn't bring James Cameron into the mix until his work matched the path Cameron had laid down in his own temp mix; Cameron would then drill down to single elements, like just the viperwolves' hunting calls, before weighing them against music and dialogue.

source.title: The Sound of Avatar

entries.text: For Quicksilver in Avengers: Age of Ultron, who appears as a disturbance of air, Boyes created thousands of fast passbys with strong doppler but gave them agitation: rather than a smooth whoosh, a percussive, stuttering texture.

source.title: The Sound of The Avengers

entries.text: Wanting Ultron's metal body to sound precise and metallic but never scrapey, Boyes found a tiny Burbank bearing supply shop, bought a large ball bearing and revolved it gyroscopically, producing about 100 tracks that he mixed together very subtly on the stage.

source.title: The Sound of The Avengers

entries.text: Ultron's voice in Age of Ultron was a year-long relay: David Acord did a first design pass, Boyes took it further with Jeff Ford, then it went to re-recording mixer Lora Hirschberg, handling dialogue, who added her own treatment.

source.title: The Sound of The Avengers

entries.text: In Age of Ultron's Atmos mix, Boyes valued bass management in the rear as well as the front: it adds power without making the track louder overall, used as Sokovia lifts into the sky and when grinding machinery starts up overhead as the heroes go underground.

source.title: The Sound of The Avengers

entries.text: Pain and Gain's main title builds a sonic signature from recorded gym equipment: elliptical machines, dumbbells, clanking 45lb plates. Aadahl and Ethan Van der Ryn laid a Bumblebee vocal effort by late collaborator Mike Hopkins over a dumbbell clank as a tribute.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Pain and Gain

entries.text: When Pain and Gain's hero speedboat couldn't be recorded in Florida due to mechanical problems, Aadahl's team recreated it with a racing boat on open water at Lake Castaic, California, riding along with the recorders as it revved.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Pain and Gain

entries.text: For Argo's revolution scenes, Aadahl brought in about a hundred extras to shout the exact Farsi slogans heard in 1979, placing mics behind windows, on rooftops, inside cars and in the middle of the crowd to capture each perspective.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of ARGO

entries.text: Archival footage showed 1979 Tehran used European two-tone sirens. Aadahl's team built a car rig with two pneumatic two-tone horns, police and ambulance, and recordist P.K. Hooker drove it around the Warner Bros. lot to capture both close-ups and distant-city siren perspectives.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of ARGO

entries.text: For Inside Out's memory orbs, which needed to feel glassy but sweet and musical, the team recorded different glasses filled with varying volumes of water to find the right pitches, then pitched them up and down, which became the sound of memories rewinding.

source.title: The Sound of Inside Out

entries.text: For Jurassic World's gyrosphere, Nelson put a mic with a wireless transmitter inside a five-gallon glass carboy and spun it on a potter's wheel, so no cable tangled. Rubbing wheels and objects along the outside captured glass resonance from inside, and he could vary the speed up and down.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Jurassic World

entries.text: For Lincoln, Burtt and recordist Greg Smith got into the White House with handheld recorders and recorded the French clocks that ticked during Lincoln's presidency, plus the mahogany doors: knocks, hardware, keys turning and opening at various forces. Those are the doors and clocks heard in the film.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Lincoln

entries.text: To record Lincoln's own pocket watch, wound for perhaps the first time in a century at the Kentucky Historical Society, Greg Smith built a small soundproof box holding the watch and a tiny Tram lavalier mic, closing the lid to isolate its ticking.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Lincoln

entries.text: With no recordings existing from 1865, Burtt rebuilt Lincoln's soundscape from historical accounts: how busy the traffic was near the White House, whether steam trains ran and how far the yards were, which church bells could be heard. Then he gathered those sounds from museums and locations.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Lincoln

entries.text: Gravity's handling and Foley sounds (loosening bolts, opening doors) were captured as transducer recordings of vibration rather than airborne sound. Lievsay says that whole layer split the difference between seeing an event and hearing it, and the reality that there's no air in space.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Gravity

entries.text: On Gravity's radio dialogue, Lievsay and Alfonso Cuarón found that the more futzed the voices, the more realistic but the less emotion reached the audience, so they kept adjusting the futz scene by scene, making it less literal when the moment needed feeling.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Gravity

entries.text: Gravity panned every voice with its actor wherever they floated, focusing the eye but also disorienting the audience. For Atmos, the essentially mono dialogue became objects carrying the 7.1 pans, then tracked even more precisely with added height.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Gravity

entries.text: Thom compares The Revenant's bear vocals to directing an actor: his first pass let the bear overact, but Iñárritu wanted it to underplay, with empty spaces rather than a growl filling every moment of the several-minute attack.

source.title: The Sound of The Revenant

entries.text: Iñárritu's made-up term 'kakaya' on The Revenant means offscreen noise you'd never design in, unrelated to the on-screen action yet believable for the location. Thom says it adds emotional resonance and realism, as long as it isn't overused.

source.title: The Sound of The Revenant

entries.text: On The Revenant, Hernández pulled sounds from production dailies not for what was said but for their resonance and acoustics, then processed them to blend with the music, treating music as part of the sound design so viewers can't tell where one ends.

source.title: The Sound of The Revenant

entries.text: To place Ratatouille in Paris subtly, Thom's team recorded background voices with real French speakers, so straining your ears reveals genuine French murmuring behind the scenes.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Ratatouille

entries.text: In Scott Pilgrim vs. the World each fight has its own punch sound. The Matthew Patel fight uses 8-bit video game impacts, but true 8-bit punches sounded weak, so Slater's team applied a pseudo 8-bit reduction while keeping weight so hits land in the gut.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Scott Pilgrim vs. the World

entries.text: When building backgrounds, even a castle interior, Nielsen's first move on Maleficent is to find the 'air': the overall feel of air and wind as a foundation. Then he adds offscreen life like people walking elsewhere in the castle, wind in trees, and strategically placed thunder.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Maleficent

entries.text: Maleficent's recurring curse got its own voice treatment, sometimes intelligible words, sometimes an ethereal whisper; whenever it returns, Atmos let Nielsen move it through the overheads and to specific spots around the sides.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Maleficent

entries.text: Maleficent's wings were hard because feather recordings tend to turn papery, leathery or creaky. Nielsen's team worked with Foley and recorded their own material, layering for feathers that still had strength and weight, revising as the effects shots changed to the end.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Maleficent

entries.text: Maleficent keeps its two worlds sonically apart: the Moors get exotic, unfamiliar birds and winds given tonal, magical qualities, while the human kingdom stays ordinary. Nielsen notes stage-shot fantasy films arrive with silence or fan and smoke-machine noise, so everything must be rebuilt.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Maleficent

entries.text: For The Princess and the Frog's 1920s New Orleans, Benitez recorded on location in the city and the swamp; the key was finding places free of modern traffic, and Royal Street, a shopping street, gave him usable period-neutral backgrounds.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Princess and the Frog

entries.text: The Princess and the Frog's riverboat resembles Disneyland's Mark Twain, so Benitez got access at 5am and recorded the real boat with six recorders at once, covering every aspect of it.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Princess and the Frog

entries.text: Resident Evil 7's ambiences were calculated against how long players linger in a room: positioned wind, rattling windows and subtle unsettling horror tones build stress gradually, and stretches of silence are protected so players imagine what comes next.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Resident Evil 7
